This report presents a rare case of localized wire migration to a subcutaneous lesion of the upper back in a breast cancer patient undergoing breast-conserving surgery. CASE SUMMARY A 48-year-old female was scheduled for breast-conserving surgery for left breast cancer. Ultrasonography guided wire localization was performed intraoperatively by surgeon to localize the nonpalpable breast cancer. After axilla sentinel lymph node biopsy, we realized that the wire was not visualized. The wire was not found in the operation field, including the breast and axilla. Breast-conserving surgery was performed after wire re-localization. Intraoperative chest posteroanterior view revealed that the wire was located on the level of midaxillary line. Two days after the operation, a serial simple X-ray revealed that the wire was located on the subcutaneous lesion of the back. The wire tip was palpable under the skin of the upper back, and the wire was removed under local anesthesia. CONCLUSION Hooked wire misplacement can lead to fatal complications. Surgeons must consider the possibility of wire migration during breast cancer surgery. Few reports have documented complications, such as wire migration, dislocation, and transection, occurring between the procedure and surgery[3,4]. A dislocated wire can migrate to unusual organs, including the heart, lung, pulmonary hilum, and abdomen, leading to fatal complications[5-8]. She underwent breast ultrasonography two years ago and at that time, there was no evidence of abmormality including breast mass. History of past illness She was in a premenopausal status. She has two children and she breastfed both of her children for more than one year. She was of normal weight, with a body mass index of 21.3 kg/m2. fetched_contents.text: Preoperative Magnetic Seed Versus Wire-Guided Localization in the Treatment of Nonpalpable Breast Cancer: A Retrospective Observational Study at a Tertiary Care Center Abstract Background: Breast cancer screening and effective neoadjuvant treatments have increased surgeries for nonpalpable tumors, often requiring preoperative localization. The wire-guided method, performed on the same day as surgery, has limitations, prompting interest in wire-free alternatives like magnetic seed devices. Methods: A retrospective single-center study (November 2020–March 2024) compared magnetic seed and wire-guided localization in 558 patients. The primary aim was to assess localization and retrieval success, resection margins, and reoperation rates. Secondary endpoints included the interval between localization and surgery, operative time, incision site selection, and volume excised. Results: Among 558 patients, 188 underwent magnetic seed and 370 wire-guided localizations. Both groups were similar in BMI, breast size, and lesion characteristics. Complications in the wire-guided group included device migration (0.5%) and hematoma (1.3%). Success rates were comparable (98.9% vs. 99.7%), as were positive margins (5.3% vs. 6.7%) and reoperation rates (6.9% vs. 7.8%). Excised volume was significantly lower in the magnetic seed group (24.2 [range 6.5–48.0 cm3] vs. 41.5 cm3 [range 16.0–68.0 cm3], p < 0.001). The magnetic seed group had an average localization-to-surgery interval of 1 day (range 0–160 days). Conclusions: Magnetic seed localization is as safe and effective as wire-guided localization, with comparable success rates and resection margins adequacy. Its primary advantage is scheduling flexibility, offering a longer interval between localization and surgery. Keywords: breast cancer, magnetic seed, magseed, nonpalpable, wire-guided 1. Introduction In recent decades, the implementation of mammographic screening programs, along with improved imaging technologies, has led to a significant increase in the diagnosis of breast cancer at a very early stage [1]. Usually, these lesions are not clinically evident and may present with different radiological features, including small nodular opacities, architectural distortion, and microcalcifications. In most cases, patients are candidates for breast-conserving surgery (BCS), provided that the target lesion is accurately localized preoperatively to allow the surgeon to perform a complete cancer clearance with adequate resection margins while preserving as much healthy tissue as possible. Similarly, the increased use of primary systemic therapy for neoadjuvant purposes (neoadjuvant systemic therapy [NAST]), even in early stage breast cancer, has expanded the indication for BCS due to its high effectiveness in tumor downsizing [2]. The response of the cancer to the preoperative treatment also raises the issue of preoperative localization of the target lesion, as it is no longer clinically evident at the time of surgery. The method commonly used for the localization of such lesions is the placement of a wire (wire guided [WG]) under ultrasound or mammographic guidance, which currently represents the standard of care due to extensive clinical experience and supporting long-term data [3]. Common limitations of wires include the risk of dislocation or migration, and difficulties in surgical scheduling, since the wire must be inserted on the same day as the surgery. Moreover, the location for wire insertion is usually selected based on the radiologist's ease, without consideration of the surgeon's preference for the skin incision site. Due to the distance between the wire entry point on the breast surface, the target lesion, and the incision site, the surgeon might be forced to perform extensive breast tissue dissection and overresection [4]. Alternative wire-free techniques have been described over time in the literature to overcome some limitations of the WG method, including techniques using radionuclides, intraoperative ultrasound, radiofrequency devices, or radar reflectors [5–9]. Among these, the use of the paramagnetic device Magseed (Endomag, Cambridge, United Kingdom) has gained popularity since its introduction [10]. Magseed (MS) is a 5 × 1 mm cylindrical device that can be inserted through a needle under local anesthesia into the target lesion with ultrasound or mammographic guidance and subsequently identified intraoperatively with a dedicated probe magnetometer (Sentimag, Endomag, Cambridge, United Kingdom). Although the literature on this subject has grown considerably in recent years [11–17], there are relatively few comparative studies between the conventional method and the use of MS [18–22]. The aim of this study was to contribute to the evidence currently available on the topic by retrospectively comparing the cases of nonpalpable breast cancer treated in our institute with the MS method to those treated with the WG method during the same period. 2. Background: While WL has been the most common approach for localization of nonpalpable breast tumors, other techniques such as RSL, intraoperative ultrasound, radioactive intraoperative occult lesion localization, hematoma localization, radar localization, and magnetic seed localization have been suggested as safe and efficacious alternatives. However, very few randomized controlled trials have compared these localization techniques. Methods: Between July 2015 and January 2021, 400 women with nonpalpable malignant breast disease were randomized 1:1 to RSL or WL, stratified by the surgeon and invasive disease status. The primary outcome was initial resection negative margin rates. Secondary outcomes included time efficiencies, cost, and satisfaction. Shared or overlapping complications across both localization methods

The evidence for shared complications is thin and mixed, but the available sources point to several common issues that can arise with both radioactive seed localization and wire-guided localization. First, minor local wound complications are mentioned for both methods: bleeding, drainage, redness, and severe pain or pressure are listed as signs that patients should contact their doctor after radioactive seed localization [N1-R3]. For wire-guided localization, minor bleeding at the insertion site is noted as a risk, and infection is described as “negligible” but still a recognized risk [N2-R2]. Although the sources do not give a direct comparison of complication rates, they do suggest that both techniques can cause minor wound-related morbidity [N1-R3][N2-R2].

A more substantive shared issue is imaging failure or loss of the marker/device, which can lead to repeat localization attempts. The wire-guided study explicitly states that complications in the wire-guided group included device migration and hematoma, and that failure or loss of the device can necessitate repeat localization [N3-F2]. For radioactive seed localization, the Annals of Surgery abstract notes that seed migration is a known drawback, and the comparative study explicitly mentions “known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty” [N4-R4]. These are not exactly the same as wire migration, but they are both device-related localization failures that can cause repeat procedures and delay surgery. The shared theme is that the marker or device may not be found at the time of surgery, requiring relocalization or reoperation [N3-F2][N4-R4].

A third overlapping category is patient discomfort, anxiety, and procedural burden. Radioactive seed localization is described as a “safe procedure with a low complication rate,” but the same source also notes that a case report published in the article indicates there can be complications [N3-R2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract reports that patients receiving RSL had better anxiety, pain, and satisfaction scores than those with wire localization [N4-F3]. For wire-guided localization, the Sirius Medical source says the technique is “widely used” but also “presents several limitations that can affect both workflow and patient experience” [N2-R3]. The UPMC source similarly notes that patients should be advised to call their doctor if they experience excessive bleeding, drainage, redness, or severe pain or pressure [N1-R3]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that both methods can cause patient discomfort and anxiety, with wire-guided localization arguably having a stronger procedural burden due to the need for same-day insertion and the physical discomfort of wire placement [N2-R3][N1-R3].

Overall, the shared complications across both localization methods include minor wound-related symptoms, imaging/device loss requiring repeat localization, and patient discomfort/anxiety. The evidence is strongest for migration or device loss as a cause of repeat procedures, but the sources do not provide direct comparative rates or a comprehensive overlap table [N3-F2][N4-R4][N2-R2].

Specific complications reported for radioactive seed localization

Radioactive seed localization is reported to have unique intraoperative and postoperative complications that distinguish it from wire-guided localization. The evidence indicates that seed migration, displacement, or failure to localize is a recognized drawback. The Annals of Surgery abstract explicitly states that known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty [N4-R4]. The Sirius Medical source adds that radioactive seed localization is considered safe with a low complication rate, but also notes that a case report published in the article indicates there can be complications [N3-R2]. This suggests that while the overall complication burden may be low, the technology-specific risks remain relevant.

A particularly important complication is radiation safety and handling. The UPMC source notes that radioactive seed localization has low radiation exposure and is “completely safe for most breast cancer patients,” but also emphasizes that radiation safety concerns and handling issues should be addressed [N1-R4][N1-R5]. The Annals of Surgery abstract similarly mentions concerns regarding radioactive contamination [N4-R4]. These sources together show that the handling of radioactive materials is a key concern, even though the radiation exposure itself is described as minimal [N1-R4][N4-R4]. The evidence does not provide detailed contamination incident rates or extensive safety protocols, so the safety concern should be treated as a procedural and institutional handling issue rather than a high-frequency complication.

The evidence also supports the idea that radioactive seed localization can fail to localize the lesion reliably. The Annals of Surgery abstract states that “known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty” [N4-R4]. This implies that failure to find the seed at the time of surgery may occur, which can lead to repeat localization attempts or reoperation. The comparative study on magnetic seed versus wire-guided localization is not directly about radioactive seed localization, but it does provide context that magnetic seed devices are used as wire-free alternatives to address limitations of wire-guided methods, including migration and hematoma [N3-F2]. Although this is not a direct statement about radioactive seed localization, it supports the broader idea that localization failure is a common enough issue in seed-based techniques to motivate alternative devices.

In terms of intraoperative and postoperative complications unique to radioactive seed implantation, the evidence is more descriptive than quantitative. The sources emphasize seed migration, inability to reposition, bracketing difficulty, radiation safety concerns, and the low but present risk of complications [N4-R4][N1-R4][N1-R5]. There is no direct evidence in the provided material of wire breakage or migration in radioactive seed localization, which is a complication more commonly associated with wire-guided localization [N2-R1]. Therefore, the unique complications reported for radioactive seed localization are best summarized as seed migration, displacement-related localization failure, radiation safety/handling concerns, and the procedural burden of bracketing and repositioning [N4-R4][N1-R4][N1-R5].

Specific complications reported for wire-guided localization

Wire-guided localization is reported to have several intraoperative and postoperative complications that are unique to the method. The most prominent is wire migration, dislocation, or misplacement. The PMC case report explicitly states that “few reports have documented complications, such as wire migration, dislocation, and transection, occurring between the procedure and surgery” [N2-R1]. It also describes a rare case in which a hooked wire migrated to the subcutaneous lesion of the upper back, requiring removal under local anesthesia [N2-F1]. This is a clear example of a serious, albeit rare, complication. The same case report notes that a dislocated wire can migrate to unusual organs, including the heart, lung, pulmonary hilum, and abdomen, and may lead to fatal complications [N2-F1]. This evidence strongly supports the claim that wire migration is a recognized and potentially serious complication of wire-guided localization.

Another unique complication is hematoma. The comparative magnetic seed versus wire-guided study reports that complications in the wire-guided group included device migration (0.5%) and hematoma (1.3%) [N3-F2]. This provides a direct quantitative context: hematoma is a relatively common minor complication in wire-guided localization. The Sirius Medical source also notes that wire-guided localization presents several limitations that can affect both workflow and patient experience, implying that procedural complications beyond migration can arise [N2-R3]. The Canadian Cancer Society description of wire localization says it is done before excisional biopsy and is a standard preoperative guidance method, but does not add much on complication frequency [N2-R5].

False-negative localization and surgical re-excision risks are also reported for wire-guided localization. The wire-guided study notes that complications included device migration and hematoma, and that reoperation rates were 7.8% in the wire-guided group [N3-F2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract states that wire localization has been the most common approach for localization of nonpalpable breast tumors, and that alternative techniques such as RSL, intraoperative ultrasound, radioactive intraoperative occult lesion localization, hematoma localization, radar localization, and magnetic seed localization have been suggested as safe and efficacious alternatives [N4-F3]. This framing supports the idea that wire-guided localization is associated with a risk of failed or false-negative localization, which can drive re-excision and repeat procedures. The same study also reports that the wire-guided group had comparable success rates to magnetic seed localization, but still had reoperation rates of 7.8% [N3-F2]. Although this is not a direct statement about false-negative localization, it is consistent with the logic that localization failure can lead to reoperation.

In addition to these complications, the evidence suggests that wire-guided localization can cause procedural burden and workflow issues. The Sirius Medical source states that the technique is widely used but presents several limitations that affect workflow and patient experience [N2-R3]. The PMC case report also emphasizes that wire migration can lead to fatal complications, reinforcing the importance of careful handling and postoperative monitoring [N2-F1]. Taken together, the unique complications reported for wire-guided localization are wire migration, dislocation, transection, hematoma, false-negative localization, re-excision risks, and workflow/procedural burden [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N2-R3].

Evidence on localization failure, repeat procedures, and outcome impacts

The evidence for localization failure and repeat procedures is strongest for wire-guided localization, with some relevant evidence also pointing to radioactive seed localization. The comparative magnetic seed versus wire-guided study reports that complications in the wire-guided group included device migration (0.5%) and hematoma (1.3%) [N3-F2]. It also reports that the wire-guided group had reoperation rates of 7.8% [N3-F2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract states that wire localization has been the most common approach for localization of nonpalpable breast tumors and that alternative techniques have been suggested as safe and efficacious alternatives [N4-F3]. This suggests that wire-guided localization is frequently used but is not immune to failure, and that failure can drive repeat procedures and reoperation.

For radioactive seed localization, the evidence indicates that seed migration is a known drawback, and that RSL has “known drawbacks of seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty” [N4-R4]. The Annals of Surgery abstract also notes that the study found no significant difference in negative margin rates between RSL and WL, but reported better patient scores for anxiety, pain, and satisfaction with RSL [N4-F3]. This implies that although seed localization may not have the same failure rate as wire localization, it can still fail to localize the lesion reliably enough to require reoperation. The evidence does not provide a direct repeat-procedure rate for radioactive seed localization, so the repeat-procedure claim must be treated as a mechanism-based inference rather than a stated statistic [N4-R4][N4-F3].

The impact on surgical workflow, re-excision rates, and patient outcomes is also evident. The wire-guided study reports that the magnetic seed group had a lower excised volume and a longer localization-to-surgery interval, while the wire-guided group had comparable success rates but still required repeat procedures and reoperation [N3-F2]. The Annals of Surgery study found no significant difference in negative margin rates between RSL and WL, but RSL was associated with better anxiety, pain, and satisfaction scores [N4-F3]. The Sirius Medical source notes that wire-guided localization presents several limitations that can affect both workflow and patient experience [N2-R3], which is consistent with the idea that localization failure can slow workflow and increase procedural burden.

Guidance on when to retry localization and how to manage failure is less explicit in the provided evidence, but it can be inferred from the study designs and complication reporting. The magnetic seed versus wire-guided study explicitly includes device migration and hematoma as complications and reports reoperation rates, which implies that failure should be managed with repeat localization or reoperation if the marker/device is not found [N3-F2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract also reports that patients receiving RSL had better satisfaction scores than those with wire localization, suggesting that patient-centered management and anxiety reduction may be part of the guidance framework [N4-F3]. The UPMC source gives a practical patient-level guidance list, advising patients to call their doctor if they experience excessive bleeding, drainage, redness, or severe pain or pressure [N1-R3], but this is more a general complication response guideline than a specific retry protocol.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that localization failure is a clinically meaningful issue for both methods, with wire-guided localization having explicit device-related failure rates (0.5% migration, 1.3% hematoma, 7.8% reoperation) and radioactive seed localization having seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty as key limitations [N3-F2][N4-R4]. The outcomes include re-excision, longer or more complex surgery, and patient-reported outcomes such as anxiety and satisfaction [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence does not provide a complete, standardized retry algorithm, but it does support the general principle that failure should prompt repeat localization or reoperation when the marker/device is not found [N3-F2][N4-R4].

## Final integrated answer on complications reported during both localization methods

The evidence in the branch reports indicates that both radioactive seed localization and wire-guided localization are associated with a spectrum of complications, some common across both methods and others unique to each approach. The overall pattern is that both techniques are generally considered relatively safe, but they each carry device-specific risks that can lead to repeat procedures, re-excision, and clinically relevant procedural burden.

---

## 1. Shared or overlapping complications across both localization methods

The shared complications reported in the branch evidence are not uniform across all studies, but they do overlap in important ways.

### Minor wound-related complications
Both techniques can cause minor wound-related symptoms. For radioactive seed localization, the UPMC source notes that patients should be advised to call their doctor if they experience excessive bleeding, drainage from the incision site, redness, or severe pain or pressure [N1-R3]. For wire-guided localization, the Westmead BCI fact sheet notes minor bleeding at the insertion site and describes infection as “negligible” but still a recognized risk [N2-R2]. These are the clearest examples of shared local wound complications.

### Imaging/device failure requiring repeat localization
A central shared issue is imaging failure or loss of the marker/device, which can necessitate repeat localization attempts. The wire-guided comparative study reports complications including device migration and hematoma, and notes that reoperation rates were 7.8% in the wire-guided group [N3-F2]. The radioactive seed literature also reports seed migration as a known drawback of RSL, and the Annals of Surgery abstract states that RSL has “known drawbacks of seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty” [N4-R4]. Taken together, these findings suggest that both methods can fail to localize the lesion reliably enough to require relocalization or reoperation [N3-F2][N4-R4].

### Patient discomfort, anxiety, and procedural burden
Both techniques can cause patient discomfort and anxiety. Radioactive seed localization is described as a “safe procedure with a low complication rate,” but the same source also notes that a case report published in the article indicates there can be complications [N3-R2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract reports that patients receiving RSL had better anxiety, pain, and satisfaction scores than those with wire localization [N4-F3]. For wire-guided localization, the Sirius Medical source states that the technique is widely used but presents several limitations that can affect both workflow and patient experience [N2-R3]. This indicates that both methods carry procedural burden and can affect patient-reported outcomes.

So, the shared complications across both localization methods include:
- minor wound symptoms such as bleeding, drainage, redness, or severe pain [N1-R3][N2-R2]
- imaging/device loss requiring repeat localization [N3-F2][N4-R4]
- patient discomfort, anxiety, and procedural burden [N3-R2][N4-F3][N2-R3]

---

## 2. Specific complications reported for radioactive seed localization

Radioactive seed localization has unique complications that are distinct from those reported for wire-guided localization.

### Seed migration, displacement, or failure to localize
The strongest reported unique complication is seed migration. The Annals of Surgery abstract explicitly states that known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty [N4-R4]. This means that the seed may not be found at the time of surgery, which can lead to repeat localization or reoperation. The Sirius Medical source also notes that radioactive seed localization is considered safe with a low complication rate, but a case report published in the article indicates that complications can still occur [N3-R2].

### Radiation safety concerns and handling issues
A key safety concern specific to radioactive seed localization is radiation exposure and handling. The UPMC source notes that radioactive seed localization has low radiation exposure and is “completely safe for most breast cancer patients,” but also emphasizes that radiation safety concerns and handling issues should be addressed [N1-R4][N1-R5]. The Annals of Surgery abstract similarly mentions concerns regarding radioactive contamination [N4-R4]. This indicates that while the radiation dose is low, the handling and institutional safety protocols are important considerations.

### Unique intraoperative and postoperative complications
The evidence supports a few unique intraoperative and postoperative complications:
- seed migration and inability to reposition [N4-R4]
- bracketing difficulty [N4-R4]
- radiation safety/handling concerns [N1-R4][N4-R4]
- low but present complications, including the possibility of a case report complication [N3-R2]

In other words, radioactive seed localization is associated with device-specific localization failure and radiation safety concerns, but the evidence does not support high-frequency wire breakage or migration as major complications for this method [N4-R4][N1-R4][N1-R5].

---

## 3. Specific complications reported for wire-guided localization

Wire-guided localization has several unique complications that are particularly relevant in breast surgery.

### Wire breakage, migration, or misplacement
Wire migration, dislocation, and transection are the most prominently reported complications. The PMC case report states that “few reports have documented complications, such as wire migration, dislocation, and transection, occurring between the procedure and surgery” [N2-R1]. It also describes a rare case in which a hooked wire migrated to the subcutaneous lesion of the upper back, requiring removal under local anesthesia [N2-F1]. The same case report emphasizes that a dislocated wire can migrate to unusual organs, including the heart, lung, pulmonary hilum, and abdomen, and may lead to fatal complications [N2-F1]. This is a strong example of a serious, albeit rare, complication.

### Hematoma
Hematoma is a common minor complication of wire-guided localization. The comparative magnetic seed versus wire-guided study reports that complications in the wire-guided group included device migration (0.5%) and hematoma (1.3%) [N3-F2]. This provides a direct quantitative context: hematoma is a relatively common complication in this method.

### False-negative localization and surgical re-excision risks
Wire-guided localization is also associated with false-negative localization and surgical re-excision risks. The wire-guided study reports reoperation rates of 7.8% in the wire-guided group [N3-F2]. The Annals of Surgery abstract notes that wire localization has been the most common approach for nonpalpable breast tumors and that alternative techniques have been suggested as safe and efficacious alternatives [N4-F3]. This framing supports the idea that wire-guided localization is frequently used but is not immune to failure, and that failure can drive reoperation.

### Workflow and procedural burden
Wire-guided localization also imposes workflow and procedural burden. The Sirius Medical source states that the technique is widely used but presents several limitations that can affect both workflow and patient experience [N2-R3]. The Canadian Cancer Society description says wire localization is done before excisional biopsy and is a standard preoperative guidance method, but it does not add much on complication frequency [N2-R5]. Taken together, wire-guided localization is associated with migration, hematoma, re-excision, and workflow burden [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N2-R3].

---

## 4. Evidence on localization failure, repeat procedures, and outcome impacts

The evidence on failure and repeat procedures is strongest for wire-guided localization, with some relevant evidence also pointing to radioactive seed localization.

### Localization failure rates and repeat procedures
For wire-guided localization, the wire-guided comparative study reports device migration at 0.5% and hematoma at 1.3%, and reoperation rates of 7.8% [N3-F2]. These are the clearest failure-related statistics in the provided evidence. For radioactive seed localization, the evidence indicates seed migration as a known drawback, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty, which implies a mechanism of failure but not a direct repeat-procedure rate [N4-R4].

### Impact on surgical workflow and re-excision
The wire-guided study reports that the magnetic seed group had a lower excised volume and a longer localization-to-surgery interval, while the wire-guided group had comparable success rates but still required repeat procedures and reoperation [N3-F2]. This suggests that localization failure can slow workflow and increase surgical complexity. The Annals of Surgery abstract reports no significant difference in negative margin rates between RSL and WL, but RSL was associated with better patient-reported outcomes [N4-F3]. This implies that failure can affect both clinical and patient-centered outcomes.

### Patient outcomes and guidance on managing failure
The evidence supports better patient-reported outcomes for RSL compared with wire localization, including lower anxiety, pain, and higher satisfaction [N4-F3]. The UPMC source gives practical patient-level guidance: patients should call their doctor if they experience excessive bleeding, drainage, redness, or severe pain or pressure [N1-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not provide a complete standardized retry protocol. The wire-guided study explicitly includes device migration and hematoma as complications and reports reoperation rates, which implies that failure should prompt repeat localization or reoperation when the marker/device is not found [N3-F2].

---

## 5. Overall conclusion

The branch evidence shows that both radioactive seed localization and wire-guided localization can be associated with complications, but the nature and frequency of those complications differ.

- **Wire-guided localization** is most strongly associated with wire migration, dislocation, transection, hematoma, false-negative localization, re-excision risks, and workflow burden [N2-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2][N2-R3].
- **Radioactive seed localization** is most strongly associated with seed migration, inability to reposition, bracketing difficulty, radiation safety/handling concerns, and low but present complications [N4-R4][N1-R4][N1-R5].
- **Shared complications** include minor wound symptoms, imaging/device loss requiring repeat localization, and patient discomfort/anxiety [N1-R3][N2-R2][N3-F2][N4-R4][N4-F3].

Overall, both methods are generally safe, but they each carry distinct risks that can lead to repeat procedures, re-excision, and procedural burden. The evidence also supports the idea that patient-reported outcomes are an important dimension of complication impact [N4-F3].
